name: Fading-fear re-entry: buy equity ETFs when an elevated VIX has fallen 15% in a week
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
V(k) = M("VIXCLS",k). Return 1 if V(0) >= 20 and V(0) <= 0.85*V(5), else 0. holdBars=10 opens a 10-bar long at the signal and ignores re-triggers while open.
rationale: Existing VIX rules buy the spike or the level; this buys the first sign that fear is being unwound while it is still elevated, when the risk premium is fat but the tail is retreating.
source: Whaley (2000) The Investor Fear Gauge, J. Portfolio Mgmt 26(3); Giot (2005) Relationships between implied volatility indexes and stock index returns, J. Portfolio Mgmt 31(3)

name: VIX Schmitt trigger: leave equity ETFs when VIX closes at 22 or more, return only once it is back to 17 or less
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
V = M("VIXCLS",0). State inPos starts as 1 (set once: if ctx.state.inPos === undefined). If inPos==1 and V >= 22 then inPos=0. Else if inPos==0 and V <= 17 then inPos=1. Return inPos.
rationale: The plain 'VIX above 20' rule whipsaws around its threshold; a hysteresis band is the standard fix and nobody has priced how much of the volatility-regime benefit survives it after costs.
source: Simon & Wiggins (2001) S&P futures returns and contrary sentiment indicators, J. Futures Markets 21(5); Schmitt trigger (hysteresis) as used in Kaufman (2013) Trading Systems and Methods

name: Confirmed dip buy: 7% off the 63-day high while the VIX curve is inverted, 15-bar hold
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
Requires i >= 62. H = max of bars[i-62..i].close. dd = bars[i].close/H - 1. ratio = M("VIX",0)/M("VIX3M",0). Return 1 if dd <= -0.07 and ratio > 1.0, else 0. holdBars=15.
rationale: A price drawdown alone is ambiguous; adding VIX backwardation separates market-wide panic (where liquidity providers are paid) from a slow grind lower.
source: Nagel (2012) Evaporating liquidity, Rev. Financial Studies 25(7); Whaley (2009) Understanding the VIX, J. Portfolio Mgmt 35(3)

name: 55-day Donchian breakout on large-cap stocks, entries allowed only when VIX is below its 126-day mean
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
State pos starts 0. calm = M("VIXCLS",0) < mean_126(M("VIXCLS",k)). If pos==0 and calm and bars[i].close > ctx.donchian(55, i-1).upper then pos=1. If pos==1 and bars[i].close < ctx.donchian(20, i-1).lower then pos=0. The VIX gate applies to entries only. Return pos.
rationale: Breakouts fail more often when implied volatility is already elevated and trending up; gating entries on a calm-VIX regime asks whether the Turtle rule's whipsaw problem is a volatility-regime problem.
source: Faith (2007) Way of the Turtle; Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012) Time series momentum, JFE 104(2)

name: VIX percentile exposure scaling: equity weight = 1 minus the VIX's 3-year percentile, remainder in SHY, weekly
rule:
Rank mode: ctx.macro(id) has no look-back, so keep any history in ctx.state, pushing the value once per rank() call; "n calls ago" means n rebalances ago. Weights are long-only and sum to at most 1.
Each call: v = ctx.macro("VIXCLS"); if null return {QQQ:0.5,DIA:0.5}. Push v to ctx.state.h. If h.length < 52 return {QQQ:0.5,DIA:0.5}. Take the last min(156,h.length) values including v; p = fraction of them <= v. e = 1 - p. Return {QQQ: e/2, DIA: e/2, SHY: 1-e}.
rationale: Volatility-managed sizing normally divides by volatility; ranking the VIX against its own history is a scale-free alternative that is invariant to the VIX's long drift.
source: Moreira & Muir (2017) Volatility-managed portfolios, JF 72(4); Fleming, Kirby & Ostdiek (2001) The economic value of volatility timing, JF 56(1)

name: Connors-style VIX stretch: buy when VIX closes 10% above its 10-day average in an index uptrend, exit above the 5-day average
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
V(k)=M("VIXCLS",k). Stretch = V(0) >= 1.10 * mean_10(V). State pos starts 0. If pos==0 and Stretch and bars[i].close > ctx.sma("close",200) then pos=1. If pos==1 and bars[i].close > ctx.sma("close",5) then pos=0. Return pos.
rationale: A short-term-trading classic that sells volume in books and courses; the VIX stretch above a short average is the entry, a rebound over the 5-day average is the exit.
source: Connors & Alvarez (2009) Short Term Trading Strategies That Work (VIX stretch idea, reconstructed as above, thresholds fixed a priori)

name: VIX-adaptive trend lookback: 50-day average when VIX is 20 or more, 200-day average when it is below
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
V = M("VIXCLS",0). L = 50 if V >= 20 else 200. Return 1 if bars[i].close > ctx.sma("close", L) else 0 (NaN sma -> 0).
rationale: A slow average lags badly in a crash and a fast one whipsaws in calm uptrends; switching the lookback on implied volatility is the textbook adaptive-trend fix and has a single fixed switch point.
source: Kaufman (2013) Trading Systems and Methods (adaptive lookbacks); Faber (2007) A quantitative approach to tactical asset allocation, J. Wealth Mgmt 9(4)

name: VIX-curve dispatch on sectors: momentum while the curve is in contango, short-term reversal when it is inverted, weekly
rule:
Rank mode: ctx.macro(id) has no look-back, so keep any history in ctx.state, pushing the value once per rank() call; "n calls ago" means n rebalances ago. Weights are long-only and sum to at most 1.
ratio = ctx.macro("VIX")/ctx.macro("VIX3M"); if either null return {}. For each symbol with >= 64 bars: mom = b[L-1].close/b[L-64].close - 1 and rev = b[L-1].close/b[L-6].close - 1 (L = bars in view). If ratio < 1.0 pick the 3 symbols with highest mom; else pick the 3 with lowest rev. Ties by symbol ascending. Weight 1/3 each.
rationale: Short-term reversals are strongest when liquidity is scarce and momentum is strongest in calm trending markets; the VIX curve is a direct liquidity-stress state variable.
source: Nagel (2012) Evaporating liquidity, RFS 25(7); Moskowitz & Grinblatt (1999) Do industries explain momentum?, JF 54(4)

name: Nominal-yield trend duration: hold Treasury and credit-duration ETFs while the 10y yield proxy is below its 100-day mean
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
y(k) = M("DFII10",k) + M("T10YIE",k) = nominal 10y yield proxy in %. Return 1 if y(0) < mean_100(y(k)) else 0 (needs all 100 values non-null).
rationale: Trend-following on the yield rather than the bond price removes the carry-and-roll noise from the price series; a falling yield trend is a rising price trend by construction, so this tests whether the cleaner input gives a cleaner gate.
source: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017) A century of evidence on trend-following investing, J. Portfolio Mgmt 44(1); Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013) Value and momentum everywhere, JF 68(3)

name: TLT and IEF below their yield-implied fair value: rolling 252-day regression residual z-score of -1 or lower
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
y(k) = M("DFII10",k) + M("T10YIE",k) = nominal 10y yield proxy in %. Requires i >= 251 and all y non-null over the window. Over k=0..251 regress z_k = ln(bars[i-k].close) on x_k = y(k) with intercept (OLS), residual e_k = z_k - a - b*x_k, s = sample std of the e_k, zres = e_0/s. State pos starts 0. If pos==0 and zres <= -1.0 then pos=1. If pos==1 and zres >= 0.0 then pos=0. Return pos.
rationale: Bond price is a deterministic function of yield plus carry and roll; a persistent price shortfall versus the yield-implied level should mean-revert faster than yields trend.
source: Cochrane & Piazzesi (2005) Bond risk premia, AER 95(1); Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst (2006) Pairs trading, RFS 19(3) (residual-reversion approach)

name: Oil/gold ratio falling over 13 weeks: hold intermediate and long Treasuries
rule:
Rank mode: ctx.macro(id) has no look-back, so keep any history in ctx.state, pushing the value once per rank() call; "n calls ago" means n rebalances ago. Weights are long-only and sum to at most 1.
Oil = ctx.macro("DCOILWTICO"); if null or <= 5 return {}. r = Oil / universe.GLD last close. Push r to ctx.state.r. If r history length < 14 return {}. chg = r / r_hist[len-14] - 1 (13 calls ago). If chg < 0 return {TLT:0.5, IEF:0.5} else {}. GLD is an input only and is never held.
rationale: The oil-to-gold ratio is a widely quoted real-time proxy for growth-and-inflation pressure on the 10-year yield; a falling ratio should favour duration.
source: Practitioner lore (oil/gold ratio tracks 10y Treasury yields; Real Vision, Hedgeye and sell-side commentary); Hamilton (2009) Causes and consequences of the oil shock of 2007-08, Brookings Papers

name: Oil/gold ratio above its 26-week mean: hold cyclical sectors, otherwise SHY
rule:
Rank mode: ctx.macro(id) has no look-back, so keep any history in ctx.state, pushing the value once per rank() call; "n calls ago" means n rebalances ago. Weights are long-only and sum to at most 1.
Oil = ctx.macro("DCOILWTICO"); if null or <= 5 return {}. r = Oil / universe.GLD last close. Push r to ctx.state.r. If history length < 26 return {SHY:1}. If r > mean of the last 26 stored r (including r) return {XLI:0.25,XLB:0.25,XLF:0.25,XLY:0.25} else {SHY:1}. GLD is never held.
rationale: Oil rising against gold is a growth signal; the same ratio that is used for bonds is used here to turn cyclical equity exposure on and off.
source: Practitioner lore (oil/gold ratio as a risk-on indicator); Hamilton (2009) Brookings Papers; Chen, Roll & Ross (1986) Economic forces and the stock market, J. Business 59(3)

name: Dollar-deflated oil above its 150-day mean: hold energy equities and commodity ETFs
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
Oil(k) = M("DCOILWTICO",k); treat Oil(k) <= 5 as null. q(k) = Oil(k) / M("DTWEXBGS",k) (oil priced in the broad dollar). Return 1 if q(0) > mean_150(q(k)) else 0.
rationale: Oil priced in dollars conflates oil demand with dollar moves; deflating by the broad dollar isolates the real commodity trend that energy earnings follow.
source: Kilian (2009) Not all oil price shocks are alike, AER 99(3); Akram (2009) Commodity prices, interest rates and the dollar, Energy Economics 31(6)

name: Oil collapse relief: after WTI falls 15% in 20 bars, hold consumer, industrial, Dow and Nasdaq ETFs for 40 bars
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
O0 = M("DCOILWTICO",0), O20 = M("DCOILWTICO",20); if O20 <= 10 or O0 <= 5 return 0. Return 1 if O0/O20 - 1 <= -0.15 else 0. holdBars=40.
rationale: Cheaper fuel is a tax cut for consumers and transport-intensive industry; markets often read oil falls as a growth scare first, so the horizon is long enough to test whether the relief channel eventually shows.
source: Kilian & Park (2009) The impact of oil price shocks on the US stock market, Int. Economic Review 50(4); Driesprong, Jacobsen & Maat (2008) Striking oil: another puzzle?, JFE 89(2)

name: Foreign-revenue stocks when the dollar has weakened over 3 months, domestic-revenue stocks when it has strengthened, monthly
rule:
Rank mode: ctx.macro(id) has no look-back, so keep any history in ctx.state, pushing the value once per rank() call; "n calls ago" means n rebalances ago. Weights are long-only and sum to at most 1.
F = {AAPL,QCOM,TXN,INTC,CAT,MMM,HON,BA} (fixed a priori, heavy foreign revenue); D = {WMT,COST,LOW,UNP,T,UNH,ABT,MCD}. d = ctx.macro("DTWEXBGS"); if null return equal weight over all 16 present. Push d to ctx.state.d. If history < 4 return equal weight over all 16 present. chg = d/d_hist[len-4] - 1 (3 months ago). If chg < 0 return 1/n on each F symbol present, else 1/n on each D symbol present.
rationale: The broad-dollar index drives translation of foreign sales; a weak dollar lifts reported earnings of multinationals relative to domestic earners. Sector-level versions have been tested, a stock-level, fixed-basket version has not.
source: Jorion (1990) The exchange-rate exposure of U.S. multinationals, J. Business 63(3); Bartram & Bodnar (2007) The exchange rate exposure puzzle, Managerial Finance 33(9)

name: Long-duration versus short-duration stock baskets switched by the 3-month change in the 10y real yield, monthly
rule:
Rank mode: ctx.macro(id) has no look-back, so keep any history in ctx.state, pushing the value once per rank() call; "n calls ago" means n rebalances ago. Weights are long-only and sum to at most 1.
L = {NVDA,TSLA,AMD,ADBE,CRM,NFLX,AMZN,META} (back-loaded cash flows); S = {XOM,CVX,JPM,BAC,T,PFE,MRK,MMM} (front-loaded). r = ctx.macro("DFII10"); if null return equal weight over all 16 present. Push r. If history < 4 return equal weight over all 16 present. chg = r - r_hist[len-4] (3 months ago, percentage points). If chg <= 0 return 1/n on each L present, else 1/n on each S present.
rationale: Equity duration theory says long-duration stocks are hurt most by rising real discount rates; the ETF-level QQQ-versus-DIA test cannot isolate this because of index composition, a stock basket can.
source: Weber (2018) Cash flow duration and the term structure of equity returns, JFE 128(3); Lettau & Wachter (2007) Why is long-horizon equity less risky?, JF 62(1)

name: Real-yield factor momentum: hold the 5 of 25 ETFs with the highest (rising yields) or lowest (falling yields) 52-week beta to weekly real-yield changes
rule:
Rank mode: ctx.macro(id) has no look-back, so keep any history in ctx.state, pushing the value once per rank() call; "n calls ago" means n rebalances ago. Weights are long-only and sum to at most 1.
Each call: r = ctx.macro("DFII10"); if null return {}. Push r to ctx.state.r and, for each symbol present, its last close to ctx.state.c[sym]. Need >= 53 stored values. For each symbol with 53 stored closes aligned to the last 53 calls: x_t = r_t - r_{t-1}, y_t = ln(c_t/c_{t-1}) for the last 52 weeks; beta = cov(y,x)/var(x). trend = r_now - r_13 calls ago. If trend > 0 pick the 5 highest betas, else the 5 lowest. Weight 0.2. Ties by symbol ascending. Symbols with fewer than 53 stored closes are skipped.
rationale: Factors trend; if real yields are in a 3-month uptrend, the assets that load positively on real-yield changes are the beneficiaries of that factor's momentum, and vice versa. It turns a macro trend into a cross-sectional bet without hand-picking sectors.
source: Ehsani & Linnainmaa (2022) Factor momentum and the momentum factor, JF 77(3); Gupta & Kelly (2019) Factor momentum everywhere, J. Portfolio Mgmt 45(3); Chen, Roll & Ross (1986)

name: Dollar-factor momentum in stocks: hold the 8 of 40 large caps with the highest (dollar rising) or lowest (dollar falling) 52-week beta to weekly dollar changes
rule:
Rank mode: ctx.macro(id) has no look-back, so keep any history in ctx.state, pushing the value once per rank() call; "n calls ago" means n rebalances ago. Weights are long-only and sum to at most 1.
Each call: d = ctx.macro("DTWEXBGS"); if null return {}. Push d to ctx.state.d and each symbol's last close to ctx.state.c[sym]. Need >= 53 stored values. For each symbol with 53 aligned stored closes: x_t = ln(d_t/d_{t-1}), y_t = ln(c_t/c_{t-1}) over the last 52 weeks; beta = cov(y,x)/var(x). trend = ln(d_now/d_13 calls ago). If trend > 0 pick the 8 highest betas, else the 8 lowest. Weight 0.125. Ties by symbol ascending.
rationale: The dollar's trend is persistent and some large caps carry a stable negative or positive dollar loading through their foreign revenue; trading the loading in the direction of the dollar trend is the factor-momentum idea applied to a macro factor.
source: Ehsani & Linnainmaa (2022) JF 77(3); Jorion (1990) J. Business 63(3); Bartram & Bodnar (2007)

name: Crypto fear as a contrarian entry for tech equities: buy QQQ, XLK, DIA, XLY and XLF when the Fear & Greed index is 24 or less, hold 20 bars
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
Return 1 if M("FNG",0) is not null and <= 24 else 0. holdBars=20.
rationale: The crypto Fear & Greed index is a daily sentiment read on speculative risk appetite; extreme fear in it has coincided with broad risk-off washouts, and the question is whether tech equity ETFs are paid for buying them.
source: Baker & Wurgler (2006) Investor sentiment and the cross-section of stock returns, JF 61(4); alternative.me Crypto Fear & Greed Index methodology

name: Real-yield breakout: after the 10y TIPS yield makes a 126-day low, hold Treasuries, gold and utilities for 30 bars
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
Return 1 if M("DFII10",0) < min over k=1..126 of M("DFII10",k) (strict new 126-bar low; any null -> 0) else 0. holdBars=30.
rationale: A fresh multi-month low in real yields is a loosening-of-conditions event that should help every long-duration claim at once; the event form tests the level-shift rather than the state.
source: Erb & Harvey (2013) The golden dilemma, FAJ 69(4); Campbell & Viceira (2001) Who should buy long-term bonds?, AER 91(1)

name: Safe-haven basket while the VIX curve is inverted: UUP, TLT and GLD from ratio of 1.0 or more until it falls below 0.95
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
ratio = M("VIX",0)/M("VIX3M",0). State pos starts 0. If pos==0 and ratio >= 1.0 then pos=1. If pos==1 and ratio < 0.95 then pos=0. Return pos.
rationale: Dollar, Treasuries and gold are the three classic havens; holding them only while term-structure inversion signals acute stress tests the haven trade as a state rather than as a reaction to a spike.
source: Baur & Lucey (2010) Is gold a hedge or a safe haven?, Financial Review 45(2); Ranaldo & Soderlind (2010) Safe haven currencies, Rev. of Finance 14(3)

name: Yield-peak rollover: after the 10y yield proxy drops 25bp from a recent peak, buy growth equities for 20 bars
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
y(k) = M("DFII10",k) + M("T10YIE",k) = nominal 10y yield proxy in %. Over k=0..62: H = max y(k), kH = the k of that max (smallest k on ties), Lo = min y(k). Return 1 if H - Lo >= 0.30 and H - y(0) >= 0.25 and kH <= 10, else 0. holdBars=20.
rationale: Growth equities carry long cash-flow duration and tend to rebound when yields roll over from a spike; requiring a prior 30bp run-up and a fresh 25bp reversal makes the event specific.
source: Weber (2018) JFE 128(3); Lettau & Wachter (2007) JF 62(1)

name: Yield-peak rollover (defensive leg): the same 25bp rollover trigger applied to Treasuries, utilities, REITs and gold
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
y(k) = M("DFII10",k) + M("T10YIE",k) = nominal 10y yield proxy in %. Over k=0..62: H = max y(k), kH = the k of that max (smallest k on ties), Lo = min y(k). Return 1 if H - Lo >= 0.30 and H - y(0) >= 0.25 and kH <= 10, else 0. holdBars=20.
rationale: Bond proxies and gold are the other side of the same rate-sensitivity trade; this pairs with the growth-equity leg so the two results show where a yield-peak rollover pays, if anywhere.
source: Campbell & Viceira (2001) AER 91(1); Erb & Harvey (2013) FAJ 69(4)

name: Macro-driver pullback buying: RSI(5) under 30 in XLE, XLU, XLF or GLD only when its own macro driver is in a supportive 100-day trend
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
Use ctx.symbol to choose the driver. XLE: ok = M("DCOILWTICO",0) > mean_100(M("DCOILWTICO",k)) (oil values <= 5 count as null). XLU: ok = M("DFII10",0) < mean_100(M("DFII10",k)). XLF: ok = M("T10Y2Y",0) > mean_100(M("T10Y2Y",k)). GLD: ok = M("DFII10",0) < mean_100(M("DFII10",k)). Return 1 if ok and ctx.rsi(5) < 30 else 0. holdBars=5.
rationale: A pullback in a sector whose fundamental driver is still moving its way is more likely a pause than a reversal; the drivers are fixed a priori from textbook sensitivities.
source: Connors & Alvarez (2009) Short Term Trading Strategies That Work; Chen, Roll & Ross (1986) J. Business 59(3)

name: RSI(2) pullbacks on 40 large caps, allowed only while VIX sits between 15 and 30
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
State pos starts 0. V = M("VIXCLS",0). If pos==0 and bars[i].close > ctx.sma("close",200) and ctx.rsi(2) < 10 and V >= 15 and V <= 30 then pos=1. If pos==1 and bars[i].close > ctx.sma("close",5) then pos=0. Return pos.
rationale: Pullback buying needs enough volatility to pay and not so much that the 200-day trend filter is a lie; a middle VIX band is the regime where short-term reversion is most often described as working.
source: Connors & Alvarez (2009) Short Term Trading Strategies That Work; Nagel (2012) RFS 25(7)

name: Dollar-surge exhaustion: after the broad dollar rises 2% in 20 bars, short UUP and long GLD, SLV, DBC, USO for 20 bars
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
d0 = M("DTWEXBGS",0), d20 = M("DTWEXBGS",20). Trigger = d0/d20 - 1 >= 0.02. Return (trigger ? (ctx.symbol == "UUP" ? -1 : 1) : 0). holdBars=20.
rationale: Dollar spikes are often liquidity events that overshoot; commodity-linked assets sold off in sympathy then recover. The short UUP leg is the direct mean-reversion bet on the same series.
source: Bruno & Shin (2015) Capital flows and the risk-taking channel of monetary policy, J. Monetary Economics 71; Akram (2009) Energy Economics 31(6)

name: Hedging-demand warning: stand aside for 5 bars when an index rises over 5 days while the VIX also rises more than 10%
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
State flatLeft starts 0. Up = bars[i].close/bars[i-5].close - 1 > 0. V0 = M("VIXCLS",0), V5 = M("VIXCLS",5). Trigger = Up and V0/V5 - 1 > 0.10. If Trigger then flatLeft=5. If flatLeft > 0 then flatLeft -= 1 and return 0, else return 1.
rationale: Rising prices with rising implied volatility mean investors are buying protection into a rally; the divergence is a long-standing practitioner warning that has never been scored as a gate.
source: Whaley (2000) J. Portfolio Mgmt 26(3); Bollen & Whaley (2004) Does net buying pressure affect the shape of implied volatility functions?, JF 59(2)

name: Rate-volatility gate on bonds (MOVE proxy): flat Treasury and credit ETFs when 20-day yield volatility is above its 75th percentile of the past year
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
y(k) = M("DFII10",k) + M("T10YIE",k) = nominal 10y yield proxy in %. dy(k) = y(k) - y(k+1). rv(j) = sample std of dy(j..j+19). Requires i >= 280. Let A = [rv(j) for j=0..251]. Return 1 if rv(0) < the 75th percentile of A (linear interpolation, A sorted ascending, index 0.75*(251)) else 0.
rationale: Bond volatility clusters and bond returns are worst in high rate-volatility states; a MOVE-style proxy built from the cached TIPS and breakeven series does not need the option-implied index.
source: Bekaert, Hoerova & Lo Duca (2013) Risk, uncertainty and monetary policy, JME 60(7); Fleming, Kirby & Ostdiek (2001) JF 56(1)

name: Breakeven breakout: after 10y breakeven inflation makes a 126-day high, hold energy, materials, commodities and gold for 30 bars
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
Return 1 if M("T10YIE",0) > max over k=1..126 of M("T10YIE",k) (strict new 126-bar high; any null -> 0) else 0. holdBars=30.
rationale: A breakout in market-implied inflation is a discrete repricing of inflation risk; real-asset ETFs should follow if the market is slow to move into them, an event study rather than a level state.
source: Gorton & Rouwenhorst (2006) Facts and fantasies about commodity futures, FAJ 62(2); Bekaert & Wang (2010) Inflation risk and the inflation risk premium, Economic Policy 25(64)

name: Cyclical sector trend gated by the yield-curve sign: XLF, XLI, XLB, XLE and XLY held above their 100-day average only while 2s10s is positive
rule:
M(id,k) = ctx.macro(id, i-k): the value known by the close of bar i-k, null if none. If any M used by the rule is null on a bar, return 0 for that bar (state-machine rules also leave state unchanged). mean_N(f) = average of f(k) over k=0..N-1 (bar i included).
Return 1 if bars[i].close > ctx.sma("close",100) and M("T10Y2Y",0) > 0 else 0.
rationale: Cyclical earnings are most sensitive to the credit cycle that the curve summarises; the rule asks whether trend-following in cyclicals is better restricted to non-inverted-curve regimes.
source: Estrella & Hardouvelis (1991) The term structure as a predictor of real economic activity, JF 46(2); Faber (2007) J. Wealth Mgmt 9(4)
